entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
Ciudadanos (Citizens), founded in Catalonia in 2006 by Albert Rivera and a group of Catalan intellectuals opposing both Catalan independence and the PP-PSOE duopoly, briefly became Spain's third-largest party (2015-2019) promising to break the political deadlock — before collapsing from 57 seats (2019 April) to 10 seats (2019 November) in a single year in one of the fastest electoral collapses in European democratic history. Ciudadanos represents the pattern of centrist 'third way' parties that rise rapidly during political crises then collapse when voters return to established parties.

Ciudadanos was founded by Albert Rivera, a lawyer and politician, as a response to Catalan nationalism's dominance of the region's political discourse. The party's Catalan origins — unusual for a Spanish unionist party — gave it credibility as defending civic rather than ethnic Spanish identity. Rivera's charisma, centrist positioning (between PP and PSOE), and anti-corruption platform drove rapid national growth after 2015.

The party's fatal strategic error came when Rivera refused to support Pedro Sánchez's PSOE government after the April 2019 election (when Ciudadanos was within 4 seats of PSOE), forcing new elections in November 2019. The second 2019 election, called as tactical masterstroke by Sánchez, saw Ciudadanos voters flee to the PP (fearing Sánchez coalition with Podemos). The 82% seat collapse in 7 months remains the most catastrophic electoral implosion of any major Spanish party. Rivera resigned, and Ciudadanos declined to 6 seats by 2023.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Ciudadanos's 82% seat collapse in a single year — from 57 to 10 seats in 2019 — is the fastest major party implosion in modern European democratic history and the definitive case study of how centrist parties can destroy themselves through single tactical miscalculations.
